To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a break down of cAMP and cGMP signaling in the brain may contribute to deficits in brain function with normal aging and in a number of age-related diseases.
cyclic nucleotide signaling deficits may contribute to brain dysfunction in aging and age-related disease and that these deficits may be manipulated to improve brain function.

there are brain region-specific changes associated with aging and AD in cAMP signaling (e.g. reduced adenyly cyclase and PKA expression/activity, reduced CREB phosphorylation), and that these changes are consistent with the hypothesis that a reduction in cyclic AMP signaling contributes to the cognitive dysfunction associated with aging and/or AD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cyclic nucleotide signaling in normal aging and age-associated diseases, particularly AD and HD, as well as the potential of cyclic nucleotide-modulating drugs to treat these conditions.
the identification and characterization of cyclic nucleotide signaling changes that occur in the normal brain and in brain regions that are vulnerable to age-related diseases such as AD and HD.
understanding cyclic nucleotide signaling in the brain and its potential role in normal aging and age related diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a reduction in cyclic AMP signaling is associated with aging and/or age-related disease in some brain regions but an increase in cyclic GMP signaling is associated with age-related disease in others.
a reduction in brain cyclic nucleotide signaling, particularly cGMP signaling, is associated with cognitive dysfunction in aging, AD, and possibly PD and HD.

cyclic nucleotide signaling in the brain is altered by aging and age-related disease, but that these alterations are not consistent across brain regions, and that the net effect is a reduction in cAMP and cGMP signaling in some brain regions and an increase in other regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cyclic nucleotide signaling in the brain is not simply reduced with age, but rather is reduced in certain brain regions while increased in other brain regions.
cyclic nucleotide signaling in brain is altered with aging and age-associated diseases and that these changes may be targeted to produce therapeutic benefit.

cyclic nucleotide signaling deficits in the aging brain may be due to an overall decrease in the synthesis of cAMP and cGMP and a reduction in cGMP levels, whereas the aging and AD brain may be characterized by an increase in cAMP signaling in the cerebral vasculature and hippocampus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cyclic nucleotide signaling changes are associated with aging, AD, and PD.

cyclic nucleotide signaling in the brain is complex and region-specific and that a reduction in cyclic AMP signaling is associated with aging and a number of age-related brain disorders, whereas cyclic GMP signaling appears to be elevated in aging and AD cerebral vessels.
cyclic nucleotide signaling changes are associated with aging or age-related diseases of brain, and these changes can be targeted therapeutically.
